title: Running a Community with Vectiq: A User Guide
subtitle: Install, configure and operate the Vectiq bot: welcome, moderation, levels, events, tickets, games and keeping it healthy
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: A practical, beginner-friendly guide to using Vectiq (github.com/lucky-edgelord/aio-vector-bot, MIT), the community-management bot for the Vector messenger, based on its documentation at lucky-edgelord.github.io/aio-vector-bot. In 11 chapters you plan and install the bot, learn the configuration file, modules and setup wizard, welcome and verify new members, moderate day to day, protect the community with link safety, image guard and Sentire, run levels and a coin economy with a shop, schedule events, giveaways and polls, handle support tickets, add games, music and feed alerts, use the dashboard, webhooks and AI assistants, and finally keep it running with restore points, updates and troubleshooting. There are 22 numbered figures, 22 numbered tables, a recap, a memory trick, an expanded ELI5 and a concept map in every chapter, a command cheat sheet in the sandbox, a final exam, and a few short Python labs that run offline in the app. Credits: the course is original and follows the public documentation of Vectiq by lucky-edgelord and the Vectiq contributors (MIT licence). The documentation credits Logiq and MEE6 for feature shape, GateBot by henk.tech for verification ideas and Sentire by JSKitty of VectorPrivacy for automod. Settings and defaults may change as the project grows, so check the live documentation for the latest values.

summary: Vectiq is a bot you run yourself. You put it on a computer that stays on, such as a Mac mini, a Linux server or a spare laptop, give it its own Vector account, and invite that account to your community. When the computer is off, the bot is off.
Use a separate account for the bot. Its key sits in a file on the computer, and the account needs strong roles in your community, so never give it your personal key.
The first install compiles a Rust core, which takes several minutes. After that, the goal is simple: the bot answers !ping.

chapters.title: Configuration, modules and the setup wizard
summary: Everything about how Vectiq behaves is in one file, config.yaml, and every setting has a comment next to it. The easiest start is the setup wizard, which asks one question per screen and writes your answers into the file, keeping the comments.
To change a setting by hand: edit the file, check it with --check, and apply it with !vectiq reload. Turning a module on or off needs a restart.
Each feature is a module with a switch. Switch off what you do not need, and its commands and background jobs stay idle.

chapters.title: Welcoming members: welcome, verification, onboarding and role menus
summary: Three modules look after a new member. Welcome greets them, verification checks they are a person, and onboarding walks them through the steps and lets them pick roles. You can use any one alone.

Welcome messages use placeholders such as the member's mention and name, and !testwelcome shows a preview. Verification offers a question, a reaction or a CAPTCHA, and a gate can hide messages from people who have not verified yet.
Role menus are messages where members react to take a role and unreact to drop it. Onboarding posts a menu built from your list of emoji and roles.

chapters.title: Moderation day to day
summary: Every moderation action is stored as a numbered case, so you can see what happened, who did it and why. Commands need the matching Vector permission, so someone who cannot time people out in Vector cannot do it through the bot either.
Warnings escalate. With the defaults, a third warning gives a one-hour timeout, and the same again at six and nine. You can change the action, the length, or turn escalation off.
The bot refuses to act on you, on itself and on the community owner, and says so instead of failing quietly.

glossary.def: A numbered record of a moderation action.
A temporary mute, up to 28 days by default.
A ban that lifts itself after a set time.
Removal that repeats whenever the member returns.

chapters.title: Protecting your community: link safety, image guard and Sentire

links: Actions | are | Log delete warn timeout

summary: Safety modules watch for trouble so you do not have to. Link safety removes links to scam, malware, phishing and tracking sites using public lists. Image guard blocks pictures you have flagged, and can score nudity with a detector. Sentire is the full automod.
They share the same actions: log, delete, warn or timeout. Staff with Manage Messages and any exempt roles or channels are skipped.
The golden rule for any new rule: start with action log, read the mod log for a few days, and only then switch to delete. No detector is perfect.

chapters.title: Levels, coins and the shop
summary: Members earn XP by chatting, and XP adds up to levels. Each level needs more than the last, so early levels come quickly. You can give a role at a level, such as a Regular role at level 5.
The economy gives every member a wallet. They earn coins from daily rewards and work, keep savings in a bank, pay each other and buy items from a shop that can sell roles.
The two systems are separate modules, so you can run either one alone.

glossary.def: Experience points from chatting; 15 to 25 at most once a minute by default.
A role granted automatically at a level.
Consecutive daily claims; each extra day adds a bonus up to a cap.

!daily pays 200; the streak continues if you claim again within 48 hours.
!shop add 1500 Supporter | text role:Supporter makes an item that gives a role.

summary: Schedule an event with one message and members RSVP with a reaction. The bot posts it in your announcements channel, reminds people before it starts, and can repeat it. Set the community's time zone once so times come out right.
Giveaways run for a set time with several winners and rerolls. Polls take two to nine options. Analytics shows messages, joins and leaves per day.
All of these are quick to run from chat, and the dashboard shows entry counts and charts.

chapters.title: Keeping it running: restore points, updates and troubleshooting

maps.title: Care

summary: A bot you rely on needs a routine. Restore points are zip snapshots of the database, config and settings, made on a schedule, before risky changes and by hand. Rolling back first makes a point of the current state, so you can undo it. The bot's key is never inside a restore point.

Run the bot as a service so it starts at login or boot: launchd on macOS, a systemd user service on Linux, a scheduled task on Windows, or Docker Compose with restart enabled. Keep copies of restore points on another machine.
When something is wrong, read the log first. Most problems are named there.

glossary.def: A background program the operating system starts and restarts for you.

keyPoints: Restore points: every 24 hours, before risky changes, by hand.

Update: git pull and rebuild, or pipx upgrade vectiq.
Logs: data/vectiq.log, journalctl --user -u vectiq -f, or docker compose logs -f.
Only one Vector bot can run per process: stop the other copy.
